L113: These white and blue ensembles are service dress uniforms for enlisted sailors in the U.S. Navy. The white cotton uniform was designed for warm weather, while the deep blue wool was intended for the cold.
L114: 
L115: 【0†Image Info】
L116: 
L117:   * ## Jean Paul Gaultier ensemble
L118: 
L119: Man’s marinière-style top (Top) Striped cotton, circa 1993, 2012.56.1, gift of Antoine Bucher.
L120: 
L121: Man’s pants (Pants) Black corduroy, circa 1991, France, 2015.89.8, gift of Michael Harrell.
L122: The marinière, colloquially known as a Breton shirt, was added to the French Navy’s official uniform in 1858. The white and dark blue horizontal stripes were designed to make it easier to see men who had fallen overboard.
L123: 
L124: Over the last 150 years, Breton stripes have become an enduring fashion motif. Jean Paul Gaultier has made the marinière a mixture of his work, using it in his menswear, womenswear, accessories, and fragrance marketing.
L125: 
L126: 【0†Image Info】
L127: 
L128:   * ## Sacai ensemble
L129: Cotton, silk, synthetic, spring 2015, Japan, 2015.37.3, museum purchase.
L130: 
L131: Military elements were key to designer Chitose Abe’s spring 2015 collection for her label Sacai. In this look, she has taken the horizontal “Breton” stripes of the French Navy and combined them with a feminine lace, a juxtaposition that both highlights and challenges the masculine and feminine qualities of each material.
L132: 
L133: 【0†Image Info】
L134: 
L135:   * ## Haas Brothers dress with “middy” collar
L136: White and red cotton, circa 1895, USA, P84.25.2, museum purchase.
L137: 
L138: In the late 1840s, a portrait of four-year-old Prince Albert Edwards wearing a miniature version of the Royal Navy “sailor suit” inspired a trend for similar ensembles in civilian children’s wear. By the 1890s, sailor dresses had become mainstays of women’s summer ensembles, designed to be worn while engaging in activities such as playing tennis or spending a day at the beach.
L139: 
L140: 【0†Image Info】
L141:   * WWII U.S. Navy W.A.V.E.S. Uniform (Left) Dark blue wool, circa 1942, USA, 84.203.1 , gift of Mrs. C.W. Vernon Jr.
L142: 
L143: In 1942, American-born couturier Mainbocher designed the uniform for the U.S. Navy’s W.A.V.E.S. (Women Accepted for Volunteer Emergency Service). He made his uniform from the same navy blue wool used for male officer’s uniforms, and it was widely lauded for its fashionable aesthetic.
L144: Chanel Ensemble (Right) Dark blue wool, off-white silk, metal, circa 1960, France, 88.72.3, gift of Elizabeth Pickering Kaiser.
L145: 
L146: Chanel debuted her tweed suit in 1953 when she reopened her couture house after World War II. She often used colorful wools and silks in the suits, but here drew on naval uniforms with deep blue and gold buttons.
L147: 
L148: 【0†Image Info】
L149: 
L150:   *   *   *   *   *   * 【0†MORE IMAGES】
L151: # School
L152: 
L153: School uniforms emerged during the 16th century at religious schools for lower-income students. They resembled ecclesiastical robes and served to instill discipline through standardization. As more elite schools adopted uniforms during the 19th century, they chose modes of gentlemanly dress to distinguish students from their religious counterparts. From this shift came the school jacket—more commonly known today as a “blazer”—as well as the use of military elements.
L154: 
L155: 【0†Open】
L156:   * ## School Installation View
L157: 
L158: Most often today, both boys and girls wear blazers, shirts, and ties. Female students pair them with a pleated skirt, while males dress in black or gray pants. The blazer includes a patch on the front pocket to identify the wearer’s school. This unifies students at school, but also makes them easily identifiable off campus.
L159: 
L160: 【0†Image Info】
L161: 
L162:   * ## Princeton University Blazer
L163: 
L164: Wool, circa 1944, USA, 2012.2, museum purchase.
L165: Schools often allow some variation in uniforms based on seniority—for example, a “Letterman” jacket for varsity athletes. The term “blazer” derives from the blazing red jackets worn exclusively by members of the rowing team at St. John’s College, Cambridge University, in 1825.
L166: 
L167: During the twentieth century, the blazer entered “Ivy style” dressing in America, as both uniform and fashion garment. Bright colors and patches identify the school and class of the wearer.
L168: 
L169: 【0†Image Info】
L170:   * ## Thom Browne Men’s Suit
L171: 
L172: Thom Browne plays with the construction and proportion of a traditional gray flannel suit—the unofficial uniform of the American white-collar worker.
L173: 
L174: Gray wool flannel, white cotton pique, circa 2006, USA, 2006.16.1, museum purchase.
L175: 
L176: 【0†Image Info】
L177: 
L178:   * McCarthy & Simon School Uniform (Left) Dark blue wool and light blue silk, fall 1927, USA, 2015.60.1, gift of Richard Fitzsimmons.
L179: The dress on the leftt was issued to female students of Marymount College during the late 1920s. Like blazers, it includes a patch with the school’s initials, but in lieu of men’s tailoring elements, utilizes a bold collar and necktie reminiscent of sailor suits. Fused with a fashionable drop-waist silhouette, students got a modern and sophisticated aesthetic.
L180: 
L181: Rudi Gernreich “Japanese Schoolgirl” Ensemble (Right) Wool, fall 1967, USA, 75.112.5, gift of Gabriele Knecht.
L182: Rudi Gernreich’s ensemble recreates the sailor-look of school uniforms. By rendering his version in an adult size with an ultra-short “mini” skirt, Gernreich endowed the look with an assertive sexuality. This highlights a tendency during the second half of the 20th century to fetishize uniforms—most often seen today in kinky Halloween costumes and pornographic films.
L183: 
L184: 【0†Image Info】
L185: 
L186:   *   *   *   * 【0†MORE IMAGES】
L187: # Athletics
L188: 
L189: Athletic uniforms visually and psychologically band a team together. They also help to distinguish one team from another. This is helpful to spectators, but also to players: uniforms ensure that a football player, for example, does not pass the ball to a member of the wrong team. Bold colors and contrasts are mainstays of athletic uniforms.
L190: 
L191: 【0†Open】
L192: 
L193:   * ## Athletics Installation View
L194: The modern baseball uniform emerged during the late 19th century. It includes a shirt or “jersey” emblazoned with a team’s name. Team names are often rendered in cursive lettering—a decorative feature that became popular during the 1930s. The uniform’s main purpose was to distinguish teams from one another. Today, teams produce replica versions of their uniforms as fan gear, a major source of revenue.
L195: 
L196: 【0†Image Info】
L197:   * Geoffrey Beene “football jersey” dress (Left) Silk and sequins, fall 1967, USA, 2015.77.3, museum purchase.
L198: 
L199: Football Uniform (Middle) Wool and cotton duck, circa 1920, USA, P84.38.1, museum purchase.
L200: 
L201: Stella Jean Ensemble (Right) Multicolor cotton, synthetic, silk, spring 2015, Italy, 2015.68.1, gift of Stella Jean.
L202: Early football uniforms did not include large pads or helmets, but they were made out of durable materials like wool or canvas to withstand the high-contact nature of the game. Here, the pants provide some padding, but not the top. Colors help distinguish teams— historically, team hues might flood a top, or simply appear in bands around the upper arm, which remains a signature element of football jerseys.
L203: 
L204: 【0†Image Info】
L205: 
L206:   * ##
L207: Spyder Active Sports, Inc., Ski suit (Left) Polyester and elastane blend, circa 2011, USA, 2011.6.1, gift of Spyder Active Sports, Inc.
L208: 
L209: Gucci (Tom Ford) Jacket (Right) Pink polyester, nylon, spandex blend, circa 1995, Italy, 2008.25.4, gift of Dorothy Schefer Faux
L210: 
L211: Ski ensembles insulate against the cold, but to help skiers achieve maximum speed, they also need to be aerodynamic. High-tech, stretchy synthetics have become standard for the sport, as seen in the Spyder ensemble at left.
L212: Bright colors, symbols, and written text display an athlete’s team and/or corporate sponsors. Tom Ford used this design strategy to overtly brand his high fashion version of a ski jacket for luxury label Gucci.
L213: 
L214: 【0†Image Info】
L215: 
L216:   *   *   * 【0†MORE IMAGES】
L217: # Work
L218: 
L219: Work uniforms are designed to identify employees of particular companies, households, or public service departments. Signifiers, such as hats, colors, and badges, indicate the wearer’s duties and sometimes serve a functional purpose as well, like a fireman’s helmet. The work uniform conveys an individual’s qualification to perform a certain task, yet may also signify that person’s lack of authority relative to his or her employer.
L220: 
L221: 【0†Open】
L222: 
L223:   * ## Work Installation View
L224: Domestic servant uniforms give employees a standardized appearance. They are also designed to strip the wearer of authority by making it immediately apparent who is the servant and who the employer.
L225: 
L226: 【0†Image Info】
L227: 
L228:   * ## uniformity-work-maid-chaffeur
L229: 
L230: Paragon Uniforms (Left)
L231: Light blue and white cotton, circa 1950s, USA, 82.151.35, gift Mrs. Jefferson Patterson.
L232: 
L233: Chauffeur’s Uniform (Right)
L234: Black cotton, circa 1930s, USA, 82.151.34 , gift of Mrs. Jefferson Patterson.
L235: In the maid’s uniform, the role of servant versus employer is achieved through the use of bright pastel blue, framed by the stark white of the cuffs, collar, and apron. In the chauffeur’s uniform, the employee’s position is made clear by a plain black coat and distinctively shaped hat.
L236: 
L237: 【0†Image Info】
L238: 
L239:   * U.S. Air Force Uniform Flight Suit (Left)
L240: Olive drab wool, circa 1940 – 1945, USA, 90.171.1, gift of Mary Jane Pool.
L241: U.S. Coast Guard Uniform Flight Suit (Right) Orange fire-resistant synthetic, circa 1970, USA, 85.66.2, gift of Captain Thomas Lutton.
L242: 
L243: As aviation factions of the armed forces developed, the workwear all-in-one became a natural uniform choice. They were quickly dubbed “jumpsuits” or “flight suits,” because paratroopers jumped out of planes in them, and pilots flew in them.
L244: The all-in-one construction made them more aerodynamic than other uniform options and also safer, because they did not have shirt tails or separate pieces that could get caught in machinery. As technology improved, fire-retardant fabrics became the norm.
L245: 
L246: 【0†Image Info】
L247: 
L248:   * New York Police Department Uniform Dark blue wool, metal, circa 1940, USA, 93.16.4, gift of Bernice Lazarus.
L249: (Hat is not official NYPD apparel.)
L250: The United States formed its first modern police forces during the mid-19th century. They were modeled after the London Metropolitan Police, established in 1829.
L251: 
L252: Uniforms were key to the success of the new organizations—they made officers immediately identifiable on the streets, which helped enforce social order. Police uniforms draw heavily on military elements in order to impart power and authority.
L253: 
L254: 【0†Image Info】
L255:   * American Red Cross Nurse Uniform (Left)
L256: White cotton, circa 1918, USA, 80.112.20, gift of Mrs. A.S. Guimaraes.
L257: 
L258: WWII Red Cross Nurse Uniform (Middle) Grey and white cotton, 1941 – 1945, USA, 91.159.1, gift of Rosalia Suarez-Solar.
L259: The nurse’s uniform (with its distinctive cap and starch white collar, cuffs, and smock) was developed during the mid-19th century to outfit students of newly formed nursing schools. The uniform blends elements of a maid’s uniform with ecclesiastical garb and a fashionable silhouette to create a look that is purposefully becoming, yet modest.
L260: 
L261: Martin Margiela Work Coat (Right) White cotton, fall/winter 1998, Belgium, 2009.37.1, gift of Gift of Stella Ishii.
L262: Long white coats were issued to all employees of Maison Martin Margiela’s studio. Such coats are a frequent uniform of the couture atelier, worn to protect fabric and clothing during production.
L263: 
L264: 【0†Image Info】
L265: 
L266:   * ## Stan Herman TWA Flight Attendant Uniforms
L267: 
L268: (LEFT) Orange and beige synthetic blend, circa 1975, USA, 2016.3.2, gift of Stan Herman.
L269: 
L270: (RIGHT) Blue synthetic blend, circa 1975, USA, 2016.3.1, gift of Stan Herman.
